cards.front: Which enzymes oxidise ethanol, and what are the products?
cards.back: Alcohol dehydrogenase converts ethanol to acetaldehyde; aldehyde dehydrogenase converts acetaldehyde to acetate, which is broken down to carbon dioxide and water. A small share is oxidised by hepatic microsomal CYP2E1, and this minor route is induced by chronic drinking.

cards.front: Why does ethanol follow zero-order kinetics, and what is the practical consequence?
cards.back: Alcohol dehydrogenase is saturated at ordinary blood levels (the supply of NAD+ is the limiting factor), so a roughly fixed amount, about 8 to 12 mL of absolute alcohol per hour, is removed whatever the level. Drinking faster than this keeps raising the blood level, and the level then falls only at this fixed rate.

cards.front: What effects go with rising blood alcohol levels in mg/dL?
cards.back: About 30 to 60: loss of inhibition, apparent excitation, mood change. About 100 to 150: mental clouding, impaired attention and gait, drowsiness. About 150 to 200: ataxia and blackouts. About 200 to 300: stupor. Higher levels: unconsciousness, and death from paralysis of medullary centres. Even small amounts slow reflexes, so driving is unsafe.

cards.front: What is acute tolerance to alcohol?
cards.back: At the same blood alcohol level, central effects are stronger while the level is rising than while it is falling. This is taken as evidence of acute tolerance.

cards.front: Why is methanol toxic, and which metabolite causes the acidosis and the eye damage?
cards.back: Methanol is oxidised to formaldehyde and then to formic acid. Formic acid is cleared slowly through a folate-dependent step, and it causes the metabolic acidosis and the specific retinal toxicity. Optic disc congestion leads to blindness, and death is from respiratory failure.

cards.front: Methanol poisoning: how does fomepizole work, and why is it preferred to ethanol?
cards.back: Fomepizole (4-methylpyrazole) specifically inhibits alcohol dehydrogenase, so methanol is not converted to formaldehyde and formic acid. It is the drug of choice because it has a longer half-life than ethanol, has no inebriating action, and its IV form allows regulated dosing. KDT 8e notes that it is not commercially available in India; ethanol, which saturates alcohol dehydrogenase at a blood level of about 100 mg/dL, is the alternative.

cards.front: Ethylene glycol poisoning: what is the antidote, and what causes the toxicity?
cards.back: Fomepizole is the drug of choice, with ethanol as the alternative. Ethylene glycol is oxidised by alcohol dehydrogenase through glycolaldehyde, glycolic acid and glyoxylic acid to oxalic acid. These products cause acidosis, cardiopulmonary complications and renal tubular necrosis.

cards.front: Short note: Disulfiram in alcohol aversion therapy

points: Inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, probably through active metabolites
Acetaldehyde accumulates when alcohol is taken
Also inhibits other enzymes (alcohol dehydrogenase, dopamine beta-hydroxylase, several CYP isoforms), so it prolongs the action of many drugs
Flushing, throbbing headache, sweating, vomiting, visual disturbance, confusion
Chest tightness, dizziness, postural fainting and circulatory collapse in severe cases
Lasts 1 to 4 hours, depending on the amount of alcohol taken
Only abstinent, well-motivated patients who sincerely want to stop
Confirm no alcohol in the previous 12 hours before the first dose
Not for patients who are still physically dependent on alcohol
500 mg daily for 1 week, then 250 mg daily (KDT); the US-approved range is 250 to 500 mg daily, taken in the morning (GG14)
Sensitisation begins 2 to 3 hours after the first dose, peaks near 12 hours and lasts 7 to 14 days after stopping
Block is irreversible; recovery needs new enzyme synthesis
Infrequent: rash, metallic taste, nervousness, malaise, abdominal upset; sedation is the commonest side effect
Small rises in hepatic transaminases; use with caution in liver disease; contraindicated in cardiovascular disease
Inhibits hepatic CYPs: slows metabolism of phenytoin, warfarin, chlordiazepoxide and isoniazid
Does not reduce craving; compliance is poor, so it is now less used
Avoid all alcohol, including hidden sources such as sauces, vinegar, cough syrups and aftershave
Some patients taking metronidazole, cefoperazone or a sulfonylurea get a milder disulfiram-like reaction after alcohol

cards.front: Short note: Methanol poisoning

points: Industrial solvent; added to rectified spirit to make it undrinkable
Metabolised to formaldehyde, then formic acid, at about one-seventh the rate of ethanol
Zero-order elimination; half-life 20 to 60 hours
Symptoms appear only after a delay of a few hours
Vomiting, headache, epigastric pain, drunkenness, tachypnoea, dyspnoea, bradycardia, hypotension
Metabolic acidosis from formic acid; delirium, seizures and coma may follow
Blurred vision, optic disc congestion, blindness; death from respiratory failure
Blood level above 50 mg/dL indicates severe poisoning
About 15 mL has caused blindness; the fatal dose is estimated at 75 to 100 mL
Quiet, dark room; support ventilation and blood pressure
IV sodium bicarbonate for acidosis: the most important measure
Fomepizole (drug of choice) or ethanol to block alcohol dehydrogenase
Haemodialysis clears methanol and formate
Calcium leucovorin (folinic acid) as an adjunct to speed formate oxidation
Saturates alcohol dehydrogenase at about 100 mg/dL blood level
Can itself cause intoxication and hypoglycaemia; needs repeated blood level monitoring

cards.front: Short note: Drugs for alcohol de-addiction

points: Begins within a day of stopping; severity depends on duration and amount of drinking
Anxiety, sweating, tremor, tachycardia, insomnia, confusion, hallucinations, delirium tremens, convulsions
Benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide, diazepam; also lorazepam or oxazepam) are preferred and tapered; benzodiazepines should not be continued beyond acute withdrawal
Opioid antagonist that blunts opioid-mediated dopamine release and the reward from alcohol
Reduces relapse to drinking and to binge drinking
50 mg daily orally, started after 7 to 10 opioid-free days; a monthly 380 mg IM extended-release form improves adherence
Nausea is commonest; hepatotoxic above 300 mg daily; contraindicated in liver failure or acute hepatitis and in patients taking opioids
Weak NMDA antagonist with modest GABA-A agonist activity (exact mechanism unsettled)
Maintains abstinence when started soon after stopping alcohol; works best in patients already abstinent; efficacy comparable to naltrexone
666 mg two to three times daily (about 2 g a day in three doses); renally eliminated, so avoid in severe renal impairment
Diarrhoea is the main side effect; also nausea, abdominal pain, itching
Aversion therapy for motivated, abstinent patients
Not for patients who are physically dependent
Topiramate and gabapentin: second-line after naltrexone or acamprosate
Baclofen (GABA-B agonist): approved for alcohol use disorder in France
Nalmefene: recommended in Europe for as-needed use to reduce heavy drinking
Ondansetron and SSRIs: negative overall, possible benefit in some subgroups

cards.front: Essay: Ethyl alcohol - pharmacological actions and pharmacokinetics

points: Ethanol made by fermentation of sugars; beverages differ in alcohol content
Medicinal use is mainly external; the pharmacology matters for intoxication and dependence
Neuronal depressant; cortex and reticular activating system most sensitive, so inhibitory control is lost first
Stages of intoxication rise with blood level (see basic card on levels)
Acute tolerance: effects greater when level is rising
Actions on GABA-A, NMDA and 5-HT3 receptors, voltage-gated Ca2+ channels and K+ channels; opioid-mediated dopamine release in nucleus accumbens
Small dose: cutaneous and gastric vasodilatation, BP unchanged
Moderate dose: tachycardia and mild BP rise; large dose: myocardial and vasomotor depression with fall in BP
Chronic use: hypertension, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias
Moderate intake raises HDL, with lower coronary risk that is lost above 3 drinks a day
Megaloblastic anaemia from interference with folate metabolism
Dilute alcohol (about 10%) stimulates gastric acid; above 20% inhibits secretion and irritates the mucosa
Lowers lower oesophageal sphincter tone; acute pancreatitis is a complication of heavy drinking
Fatty liver is reversible; prolonged exposure can progress to fibrosis and cirrhosis
Diuresis from fluid intake and inhibition of ADH
Acute intoxication causes hypoglycaemia by inhibiting gluconeogenesis
Chronic use: impotence, testicular atrophy, gynaecomastia, infertility
Rapid absorption from the intestine; gastric emptying governs the rate
Distributed in total body water; crosses the BBB and placenta
About 98% oxidised in the liver, mainly by ADH then ALDH
Breath alcohol is about 0.05% of blood level; basis of breath analysers

cards.front: Essay: Acute and chronic alcohol toxicity

points: Nausea, vomiting, flushing, hangover
Road traffic accidents
Unresponsiveness, stupor, hypotension, respiratory depression, collapse, coma, death
First priorities: patent airway, prevent aspiration, ventilate if needed
Analeptics are contraindicated because they can cause convulsions
Correct hypoglycaemia with glucose; give thiamine with it; maintain fluid and electrolytes
Tolerance is pharmacokinetic and cellular, usually of low degree
Neurological: polyneuritis, Wernicke's encephalopathy, Korsakoff's psychosis, seizures, loss of brain mass
Organ damage: cirrhosis, hypertension, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias, pancreatitis, myopathy
Higher risk of oropharyngeal, oesophageal and hepatic cancer; depressed immunity
Round-the-clock drinking is needed for dependence
Nutritional deficiency, especially thiamine, is common
Genetic factors contribute to progression from social drinking to alcoholism in about half of individuals
Starts within a day; severity relates to duration and amount
Anxiety, tremor, tachycardia, hallucinations, delirium tremens, convulsions, collapse
Supportive care plus benzodiazepines
Foetal alcohol syndrome: growth retardation, low IQ, microcephaly, facial abnormalities, immune impairment
Heavy drinking also raises miscarriage, stillbirth and low birth-weight risk

cards.front: Classify: forms of alcohol
cards.text: Absolute alcohol is {{99% w/w}} ethanol; rectified spirit is {{90% w/w}} ethanol; methylated spirit contains {{5 parts}} of wood naphtha per {{95 parts}} of rectified spirit and is tinted blue with {{methylene blue}}.

cards.front: Classify: alcoholic beverages by typical alcohol content
cards.text: Malted liquors such as beer contain about {{3 to 6%}}; light wines such as claret about {{9 to 12%}}; champagne about {{12 to 16%}}; fortified wines such as port about {{16 to 22%}}.

cards.front: Classify: methanol poisoning treatment steps
cards.text: {{Sodium bicarbonate}} infusion corrects the acidosis; {{fomepizole}} is the drug of choice; {{haemodialysis}} clears methanol and formate; {{calcium leucovorin}} hastens formate oxidation.

cards.front: Which opioid receptor types exist, and what does each mainly mediate?
cards.back: Mu receptors mediate most morphine actions: supraspinal and spinal analgesia, respiratory depression, euphoria, miosis, sedation and constipation; the endogenous ligands are endomorphins, and beta-endorphin acts mainly here too. Kappa receptors give spinal analgesia with a lower ceiling, dysphoria, psychotomimetic effects and sedation; the endogenous ligand is dynorphin. Delta receptors are linked to the affective component of analgesia, reinforcement, dependence and proconvulsant action; enkephalins bind here.

cards.front: How does morphine produce spinal analgesia?
cards.back: It acts on mu receptors in the substantia gelatinosa of the dorsal horn and reduces release of excitatory transmitters, such as glutamate and substance P, from primary pain afferents. It also reduces postsynaptic excitation of dorsal horn neurones. Supraspinal action on the periaqueductal grey and descending pathways adds to this, and together they greatly amplify analgesia.

cards.front: Why does morphine cause constipation, and does tolerance develop to it?
cards.back: Mu receptors on the enteric plexus raise segmental tone and reduce propulsive movement, with spasm of the pyloric, ileocaecal and anal sphincters. Intestinal secretion falls and fluid is absorbed from stasis; a central effect also blunts the defecation reflex. No tolerance develops, so chronic users stay constipated. Miosis and the proconvulsant effect also do not show tolerance.

cards.front: Morphine respiratory depression: which drives are lost first, and which centre is most sensitive?
cards.back: The neurogenic drive is depressed first, then the hypercapnic drive, and later the hypoxic drive. Rate and tidal volume fall in a dose-dependent way, and a patient can lose the urge to breathe. The cough centre is more sensitive than the respiratory centre. Death from overdose is from respiratory failure.

cards.front: Name the main precautions and contraindications for morphine.
cards.back: Respiratory insufficiency (emphysema, cor pulmonale, pulmonary fibrosis): risk of sudden death. Bronchial asthma: histamine release can trigger an attack. Head injury: CO2 retention raises intracranial pressure and the drug masks neurological assessment. Hypotension or hypovolaemia: exaggerated fall in BP. Undiagnosed acute abdominal pain: can aggravate biliary colic, pancreatitis or diverticulitis. Elderly men: urinary retention. Infants and the elderly: more respiratory depression.

cards.front: Morphine pharmacokinetics: oral bioavailability, metabolites and half-life.
cards.back: Oral bioavailability is about one-quarter of the parenteral dose because of high first-pass metabolism. It is conjugated mainly to morphine-6-glucuronide, which is more potent than morphine at mu receptors and accumulates on chronic dosing, and to morphine-3-glucuronide, which is neuroexcitatory. Plasma half-life is 2 to 3 hours; effect lasts 4 to 6 hours; enterohepatic recirculation prolongs the stay; it crosses the placenta.

cards.front: Morphine poisoning: what is the specific antidote and why must it be repeated?
cards.back: Naloxone, given after the airway is secured and ventilation started. Dose: 0.4 to 0.8 mg IV repeated every 2 to 3 minutes until breathing recovers (maximum about 10 mg). It can also be given IM or SC, or by first responders as a 4 mg nasal spray. It is a pure antagonist with no agonist action of its own. Its action (1 to 3 hours) is shorter than that of many opioids, so the patient can slip back into coma: repeat doses every 1 to 4 hours or an infusion may be needed. In dependent users it precipitates withdrawal.

cards.front: Naloxone versus naltrexone: how do they differ?
cards.back: Both are pure opioid antagonists. Naloxone is inactive orally because of high first-pass metabolism, so it is given IV, IM, SC or as a nasal spray; it acts in 2 to 3 minutes and lasts 1 to 3 hours, which suits emergencies. Naltrexone is orally active, more potent and acts for 1 to 2 days, so it suits opioid blockade after detoxification (50 mg daily; a monthly IM depot form also exists) and relapse prevention in alcohol dependence. High doses of naltrexone are hepatotoxic.

cards.front: Fentanyl: potency, onset, duration and clinical routes.
cards.back: About 80 to 100 times morphine's potency for analgesia and respiratory depression, with few cardiovascular effects at analgesic doses and less histamine release. It is very lipid-soluble: IV onset is about 5 minutes, but the effect wears off in 30 to 40 minutes by redistribution (elimination half-life about 4 hours). Used IV in anaesthesia; transdermal patches (changed every 3 days) for cancer and chronic pain; buccal use is possible, but oral use is poor because of first-pass metabolism.

cards.front: Tramadol: mechanism of analgesia and key cautions.
cards.back: A weak mu agonist that also inhibits noradrenaline and serotonin reuptake and increases 5-HT release. Its O-demethylated metabolite, formed by hepatic CYPs including CYP2D6, is several times more potent at mu receptors and contributes to analgesia. Analgesia is only partly reversed by naloxone. Oral bioavailability is good; half-life 5 to 6 hours; respiratory depression and constipation are minimal. Cautions: lowers the seizure threshold (avoid in epilepsy) and can cause serotonin syndrome with SSRIs. Used for mild to moderate pain; not effective in severe pain.

cards.front: Buprenorphine: why is it called a partial agonist, and what are its practical features?
cards.back: It has high affinity but low intrinsic activity at mu receptors, so analgesia and respiratory depression reach a ceiling; in highly morphine-dependent people it can precipitate withdrawal. It is about 25 times as potent as morphine, lipid-soluble, with slow onset and long duration (terminal half-life about 40 hours); sublingual use is effective. It causes less tolerance and dependence than morphine, and its ceiling on respiratory depression makes it safer than methadone for opioid substitution (4 to 16 mg daily transmucosally); a combination with naloxone deters dissolving and injecting the tablets. Naloxone only partly reverses it. Avoid in labour: neonatal respiratory depression cannot be effectively reversed by naloxone.

cards.front: Methadone: why is it used for opioid substitution and maintenance?
cards.back: A full mu agonist (its racemate also blocks NMDA receptors) with a high oral to parenteral activity ratio (about 1:2) and firm tissue binding. It accumulates on repeated dosing, so the half-life on chronic use is about 24 to 48 hours, and withdrawal is slower in onset, milder and more prolonged. Detoxification: 1 mg oral methadone replaces about 4 mg morphine, 2 mg heroin or 20 mg pethidine; after 2 to 3 days of substitution it is gradually withdrawn (GG14: start 20 to 30 mg, then reduce by about 20% a day). Maintenance: KDT gives 40 to 80 mg daily orally; GG14 starts at 20 mg daily and titrates to 60 to 80 mg daily. Unlike other opioids it prolongs the QT interval. Rifampicin and phenytoin induce its metabolism (CYP3A4, CYP2B6) and can precipitate withdrawal.

cards.front: Codeine: why is it weaker than morphine, and what dose gives the antitussive effect?
cards.back: A weak partial mu agonist with low affinity and a low ceiling; analgesic potency about one-tenth of morphine, so it suits only mild to moderate pain. Much of its analgesia depends on conversion to morphine by CYP2D6, which is polymorphic: poor metabolisers get little analgesia, while ultra-rapid metabolisers form unexpectedly high morphine levels, causing respiratory depression and deaths, including breastfed infants of such mothers. Routine use in children is therefore being abandoned in the USA. Cough is suppressed at subanalgesic doses of about 10 to 30 mg. Constipation is prominent when used for pain; abuse liability is low.

cards.front: Tapentadol versus tramadol: what is the main mechanistic difference?
cards.back: Both are atypical centrally acting analgesics with weak mu activity and monoamine reuptake effects. Tapentadol inhibits noradrenaline reuptake more than serotonin reuptake, so its analgesia works mainly through noradrenergic pathways. Nausea and vomiting appear less troublesome. Like tramadol, it can cause serotonin syndrome with SSRIs and can precipitate seizures in predisposed patients. Used for moderately severe pain; comparative efficacy with tramadol is not firmly established.

cards.front: Pentazocine: why is it an agonist-antagonist, and why is it less used now?
cards.back: A kappa agonist with weak mu antagonism. Its analgesia has a lower ceiling and is mainly spinal. At higher doses it causes tachycardia and rise in BP, and dysphoric or psychotomimetic effects (believed to be sigma-mediated), which limit use. It precipitates withdrawal in morphine-dependent people. Now mainly used for postoperative and moderately severe pain.

cards.front: Short note: Clinical uses of morphine

points: Severe pain of most types: visceral, ischaemic (myocardial infarction), burns, trauma, postoperative, cancer, renal colic
Gives symptomatic relief only; assess the patient before strong analgesia, especially in acute abdomen
Neuropathic pain responds poorly; pregabalin, amitriptyline and duloxetine are the main options
IV morphine in acute left ventricular failure or pulmonary oedema: lowers preload, shifts blood from lungs, reduces dyspnoea and sympathetic drive
Useful in MI to allay apprehension; contraindicated in bronchial asthma
Epidural 2 to 3 mg or intrathecal 0.2 mg gives segmental analgesia lasting about 12 hours
Delayed respiratory depression can occur as the drug ascends the subarachnoid space
Patient-controlled IV analgesia (fentanyl) for postoperative pain
Balanced anaesthesia and premedication in selected patients
Codeine or its substitutes for dry, irritating cough
Codeine and other opioids for diarrhoea; loperamide and diphenoxylate are dedicated antidiarrhoeals
Sustained-release oral morphine or transdermal fentanyl for cancer pain, with a rescue dose for breakthrough pain

cards.front: Short note: Pethidine versus fentanyl

points: Pethidine: about one-tenth of morphine's analgesic potency, but its maximal efficacy approaches that of morphine
Fentanyl: about 80 to 100 times as potent as morphine
Pethidine IM: faster onset than morphine but shorter duration, 2 to 4 hours
Fentanyl IV: peak analgesia in minutes; short effect from redistribution; long-acting only as transdermal patch
Pethidine: atropine-like dry mouth, blurred vision, tachycardia; less miosis, constipation and urinary retention; contractility may fall
Fentanyl: few cardiovascular effects at analgesic doses; low histamine release
Pethidine: hydrolysed to meperidinic acid; norpethidine accumulates and causes tremor, myoclonus, convulsions, especially in renal failure
Pethidine interacts with MAO inhibitors and SSRIs (serotonin syndrome); fentanyl oral use is poor
Pethidine: now declined as a morphine substitute; used for shivering after anaesthesia; not useful for cough or diarrhoea
Fentanyl: anaesthesia, transdermal and buccal use for cancer and chronic pain

cards.front: Short note: Opioid antagonists and their clinical uses

points: Competitive antagonist at all opioid receptors, most potent at mu
No agonist action; no effect in people not taking opioids; inactive orally; given IV, IM, SC or as a nasal spray (usable by lay people)
Morphine and other opioid poisoning; neonatal opioid apnoea (small dose into umbilical cord)
Reverses opioid respiratory depression after surgery in small doses
Diagnosis of opioid dependence by precipitated withdrawal; adjunct for intraspinal opioid analgesia
Naltrexone: oral, lasts 1 to 2 days; monthly IM depot; opioid blockade and alcohol relapse prevention; nausea, headache; hepatotoxicity at high dose
Nalmefene: longer acting, higher oral bioavailability, less hepatotoxicity; recommended in Europe for as-needed use to cut heavy drinking
Methylnaltrexone does not cross the BBB; relieves opioid-induced constipation
Naloxegol and naldemedine: oral peripherally restricted antagonists for opioid-induced constipation
Alvimopan: limited gut absorption; approved for postoperative ileus after bowel resection

cards.front: Short note: Agonist-antagonist and partial agonist opioids

points: Agonist at one receptor type, antagonist at another; limited efficacy and low ceiling for respiratory depression
Less addicting; but must not be given to someone on a full agonist, as analgesia can drop or withdrawal can follow
First opioid antagonist (1951) able to reverse morphine; kappa agonism
Not used clinically because of dysphoric and psychotomimetic effects
Both are kappa agonists with weak mu antagonism; ceiling effect on analgesia and respiratory depression
Butorphanol: parenteral only; about 2 mg equals 30 mg pentazocine; avoid in cardiac ischaemia
Nalbuphine: parenteral; little sympathetic stimulation; can precipitate withdrawal in morphine dependence; usable in MI
Partial mu agonist, about 25 times morphine potency; sublingual and transdermal forms
Precipitates withdrawal in highly dependent people; used in cancer pain and as an alternative to methadone

cards.front: Short note: Endogenous opioid peptides

points: Endorphins: beta-endorphin (31 amino acids) from POMC, which also gives ACTH and MSH; mainly mu agonist
Enkephalins: met- and leu-enkephalin pentapeptides; met-enkephalin equal at mu and delta; leu-enkephalin prefers delta
Dynorphins: derived from prodynorphin; prefer kappa, also act at mu and delta
Modulate pain, mood, reward, emesis, motor behaviour, pituitary hormones and GI motility
Beta-endorphin in the hypothalamus-pituitary axis: lowers LH and FSH; raises GH and prolactin
Naloxone blocks placebo, acupuncture and stress-induced analgesia
Naloxone reverses the hormone changes, suggesting the system is constitutively active
Acts at the NOP receptor; can act as an antiopioid at some sites
Role in stress, reward, learning and pain control depends on site and pain state

cards.front: Essay: Morphine - pharmacology, toxicity and management

points: Prototype opioid; the principal phenanthrene alkaloid of opium (about 10% of opium)
Acts mainly as a full mu agonist with the highest affinity among the receptor types
Analgesia: suppresses both pain perception and the distress it causes; spinal and supraspinal
Sedation without ataxia; euphoria through dopamine release in nucleus accumbens; calming effect
Respiratory and cough depression; miosis; truncal rigidity at high IV doses; lowers seizure threshold
CVS: vasodilatation (histamine release, direct, vasomotor depression); little direct heart effect; reduced cardiac work
GIT: constipation through spasm and reduced propulsion; biliary spasm; urinary retention
Histamine release can cause bronchoconstriction, a concern in asthma
Poor and variable oral bioavailability (about one-quarter of parenteral); about 30% protein bound
Glucuronide conjugation in liver; M6G is active; half-life 2 to 3 hours
Tolerance to most actions, but not to constipation, miosis or convulsions
High abuse liability; withdrawal with lacrimation, yawning, sweating, restlessness, diarrhoea, insomnia and rise in BP; delirium uncommon
Stupor, pinpoint pupils, shallow breathing, hypotension; death from respiratory failure
Ventilatory support, BP maintenance, and naloxone IV repeated as needed

cards.front: Essay: Opioid dependence - mechanisms, withdrawal and treatment

points: Tolerance is mainly pharmacodynamic (cellular) with some pharmacokinetic contribution
Dependence linked to mu-receptor activation and the dopamine reward pathway
In animals, NMDA antagonists and nitric oxide synthase inhibitors block tolerance and dependence
Drug-seeking, lacrimation, sweating, yawning, anxiety, restlessness, mydriasis, tremor, insomnia, colic, diarrhoea, dehydration, palpitation
Delirium and convulsions are uncommon; death is rare with supportive care
Opioid antagonists such as naloxone precipitate withdrawal in dependent people
Stop the opioid and substitute oral methadone (about 1 mg for 4 mg morphine); after 2 to 3 days, withdraw methadone gradually
Buprenorphine can also be used to manage detoxification
Clonidine or lofexidine (central alpha-2 agonists) relieve the autonomic symptoms of withdrawal but not aches or craving; postural hypotension is common
A protracted withdrawal phase with anxiety, insomnia and craving can last up to 6 months

Long-term oral methadone (KDT 40 to 80 mg daily; GG14 titrates to 60 to 80 mg daily) creates tolerance so the high from injected opioids is lost; long-term maintenance gives better outcomes than detoxification alone
Buprenorphine (partial agonist, 4 to 16 mg daily transmucosally) is safer because respiratory depression has a ceiling; combined with naloxone to deter injection
Naltrexone after about 7 opioid-free days: oral 50 mg daily or a monthly extended-release depot
Relapse rate among post-addicts is high; long-term support is needed
Buprenorphine can precipitate withdrawal, so patients must be abstinent from other opioids before it is started
Naloxone nasal spray allows emergency reversal of overdose by people without medical training

cards.front: Essay: Opioid analgesia in chronic and cancer pain

points: Opioids relieve symptoms, not the cause; pain can be diagnostically useful
Terminal and cancer pain should not be restricted by fear of dependence
Neuropathic pain responds less predictably to opioids
Mild pain: aspirin-like drugs (NSAIDs) first
If not effective: codeine, tramadol or tapentadol, alone or with paracetamol
Moderate to severe pain: a strong opioid, often with an NSAID to keep the opioid dose low
Continuous long-acting opioid works better than intermittent short-acting doses
Oral sustained-release morphine; doses rise as tolerance develops
Methadone or opioid rotation may help when morphine fails
Transdermal fentanyl changed every 3 days gives steady levels after about 12 hours
Buprenorphine sublingual or transdermal for chronic cancer pain
Rescue short-acting opioid added for breakthrough pain
Watch for constipation, sedation and respiratory depression
Use caution in elderly, renal and hepatic impairment

cards.front: Classify: opioid receptor types and endogenous ligands
cards.text: {{Mu}} receptors mediate most of morphine's actions; {{kappa}} receptors bind {{dynorphin}} and {{delta}} receptors bind {{enkephalins}}.

cards.front: Classify: antagonists, mixed agonist-antagonists and partial agonists
cards.text: Pure antagonists include {{naloxone}}, {{naltrexone}} and {{nalmefene}}; mixed agonist-antagonists include {{pentazocine}}, {{butorphanol}} and {{nalbuphine}}; {{buprenorphine}} is a partial mu agonist.

cards.front: Classify: potency and duration of synthetic opioids
cards.text: Fentanyl is about {{80 to 100 times}} as potent as morphine with an elimination half-life of about {{4 hours}}; {{remifentanil}} is hydrolysed by plasma {{esterases}}, so its action lasts only {{10 to 15 minutes}} after IV dosing.

cards.front: Classify: half-life and reversibility of methadone and tramadol
cards.text: Methadone's plasma half-life on chronic use is {{24 to 48 hours}}; tramadol's half-life is {{5 to 6 hours}}; tramadol's analgesia is only {{partly}} reversed by naloxone.

cards.front: Classify: peripheral opioid antagonists
cards.text: {{Methylnaltrexone}} does not cross the {{blood-brain barrier}} and relieves {{opioid-induced constipation}}; {{alvimopan}} is a peripheral antagonist approved for {{postoperative ileus}}.

cards.front: Classify: codeine features
cards.text: Codeine is converted to morphine by {{CYP2D6}}; antitussive doses are about {{10 to 30 mg}}; its oral to parenteral activity ratio is about {{1:2}}.

cards.front: Classify: tolerance pattern and naloxone dosing for morphine poisoning
cards.text: Tolerance develops to most morphine actions but not to {{constipation}}, {{miosis}} or {{proconvulsant}} effects; naloxone for poisoning is {{0.4 to 0.8 mg}} IV, repeated every {{2 to 3 minutes}}.

cards.front: Strychnine: mechanism of convulsions and the type of convulsion produced.
cards.back: It blocks glycine-mediated postsynaptic inhibition, notably at the Renshaw cell to motoneurone junction in the spinal cord, so antagonist muscles also fire. Convulsions are reflex, tonic-clonic and symmetrical. Poisoning is managed like status epilepticus.

cards.front: Picrotoxin: site of action, type of convulsion and antidote.
cards.back: It is a non-competitive GABA-A blocker: it acts at an allosteric site and prevents chloride channel opening, so presynaptic GABA inhibition is lost. Convulsions are clonic, spontaneous and asymmetrical, with vomiting and autonomic stimulation. Diazepam, which enhances GABA-ergic transmission, is the drug of choice for poisoning.

cards.front: Methylphenidate: mechanism, main use and why it is preferred to amphetamine in children with ADHD.
cards.back: It inhibits the noradrenaline and dopamine transporters (NET and DAT) and, unlike amphetamine, is not a substrate for them (KDT describes it, like amphetamine, as a releaser of NA and DA). It increases mental activity at doses with little peripheral action. In children with ADHD it is preferred to amphetamine because it causes less tachycardia and growth retardation. Also used for adult attention deficit and narcolepsy; not for depression, dementia, obesity or staying awake. Half-life 4 to 6 hours, but central effects last longer, so twice-daily dosing is enough. Side effects: anorexia, insomnia, growth retardation, abdominal discomfort.

cards.front: Atomoxetine: mechanism, main use and key interactions.
cards.back: A selective noradrenaline reuptake inhibitor, unrelated to amphetamine; it does not enhance dopamine release. Used in ADHD in children over 6 years and in adults with attention problems. It is hydroxylated by CYP2D6, which is polymorphic, so CYP2D6 inhibitors (fluoxetine, paroxetine, quinidine) raise levels. Contraindicated with MAO inhibitors and in glaucoma. Dyspepsia and anorexia are the common side effects.

cards.front: Modafinil: indications, mechanism and main adverse effects.
cards.back: Approved for daytime sleepiness in narcolepsy, sleep apnoea syndrome and shift-work disorder; used to improve alertness. Its mechanism is not fully known: it inhibits noradrenaline and dopamine uptake and alters glutamate and GABA. Common adverse effects: insomnia and headache; dependence is possible with long-term use. Elimination half-life about 15 hours.

cards.front: Caffeine as a CNS stimulant: uses and toxicity.
cards.back: Caffeine has no analgesic action of its own; in analgesic mixtures it helps by countering fatigue and boredom. In migraine it is combined with ergotamine, probably by enhancing vasoconstriction and ergotamine absorption. Used as an alternative to theophylline for apnoea of prematurity. Toxicity is an extension of its actions: nervousness, insomnia, tremor, rigidity, fever, delirium, convulsions at high doses; tachycardia. Avoid in peptic ulcer. Plasma half-life 3 to 6 hours.

cards.front: Short note: Cholinesterase inhibitors in Alzheimer's disease

points: Cholinergic deficit is the most consistent neurotransmitter loss in Alzheimer's disease
Precursor loading (choline, lecithin) fails; older anti-ChEs help but cause peripheral side effects
Tacrine: first centrally acting anti-ChE, withdrawn because of hepatotoxicity
Rivastigmine: lipid-soluble carbamate; inhibits AChE and BuChE; mild-to-moderate AD only; twice-daily dosing; transdermal form available
Donepezil: reversible, CNS-selective; long half-life (about 70 hours) allows once-daily bedtime dosing; usable in more severe AD; not hepatotoxic
Galantamine: natural alkaloid; selective central AChE inhibitor with direct nicotinic agonism; twice-daily dosing
Modest symptomatic benefit in at least half of mild-to-moderate patients; cognitive decline slowed, not prevented
Stop if no benefit after about 3 months of therapy
Also used in other dementias with cholinergic deficit, such as dementia with Lewy bodies and vascular dementia
Diarrhoea, anorexia, nausea, muscle cramps, fatigue, insomnia, vivid or abnormal dreams, hallucinations
Use with caution in bradycardia or syncope
Largely similar among the three agents still in use

cards.front: Short note: Memantine

points: NMDA receptor antagonist related to amantadine
Non-competitive and use-dependent; blocks glutamate excitotoxicity
Moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease; slows functional decline
Benefit in mild disease is unclear; may replace or be added to an anti-ChE
Also used in other dementias; explored in parkinsonism
Start 5 mg once daily and increase gradually to 10 mg twice daily
Stop if no clinical benefit after 6 months
Constipation, tiredness, headache, dizziness, drowsiness; better tolerated than anti-ChEs
Symptomatic effect similar to or less than anti-ChEs

cards.front: Short note: Cognition enhancers with unproven benefit

points: Nootropic drugs claimed to improve higher cerebral function
Claimed mechanisms: cerebral blood flow, neuronal metabolism, neurotransmission, specific memory functions
Global vasodilatation may even harm in stroke by worsening oedema and causing steal
Cyclic GABA derivative without GABA-like action; not a vasodilator
A Cochrane review (2004) did not support its use in dementia; approved in UK only as adjunct for cortical myoclonus
Two pyridoxine molecules joined by a disulfide bridge; no vitamin B6 activity
Claimed to increase glucose transport across the BBB; benefit uncertain; withdrawn in some countries
Citicoline: choline and cytidine compound; short-term benefit in some studies, little convincing evidence
Ginkgo biloba: PAF antagonist; Cochrane review (2007) found only minor, inconsistent benefit; increased bleeding risk
Dihydroergotoxine: ergot alkaloid with alpha-adrenergic blocking action; therapeutic value not established
Piribedil: dopamine agonist; claims for memory and giddiness unsubstantiated

cards.front: Essay: Alzheimer's disease - pathology and drug management

points: Progressive neurodegenerative disease; most common cause of dementia in older people
Memory, problem solving, daily functioning and emotional control are primarily affected
Can progress to a vegetative state
Extracellular amyloid (senile) plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles of tau
Atrophy of cortical and subcortical areas; neuron loss
Marked cholinergic deficit; glutamate and neuropeptide systems also affected
Anti-ChEs (rivastigmine, donepezil, galantamine): modest, short-lasting benefit; do not change progression
Memantine: for moderate-to-severe disease, alone or added to an anti-ChE
Cholinergic agonists (arecoline, bethanechol) and older anti-ChEs give peripheral side effects
Anti-amyloid antibody therapy (aducanumab) for MCI or mild dementia with proven amyloid; see separate card
Reduced cerebral blood flow in AD is probably a consequence of neuron loss, not the cause
Vasodilators are not shown to help; cognitive enhancers mostly lack proof
Tacrine withdrawn because of hepatotoxicity
Reassess after about 3 months; stop if no benefit
Watch for GI upset, sleep problems and hallucinations

cards.front: Classify: convulsants by mechanism
cards.text: Strychnine blocks {{glycine}}-mediated inhibition; picrotoxin blocks {{GABA-A}} chloride channels at an {{allosteric}} site; bicuculline is a {{competitive}} GABA-A antagonist used only as a {{research tool}}.

cards.front: Classify: anticholinesterases for Alzheimer's disease by dosing and safety
cards.text: Donepezil has a half-life of about {{70 hours}} and is given {{once daily at bedtime}}; rivastigmine and galantamine need {{twice-daily}} dosing; {{tacrine}} was withdrawn because of {{hepatotoxicity}}.

cards.front: Dextropropoxyphene: what was it, and what is its current status?
cards.back: A weak synthetic opioid chemically related to methadone, about half as potent as codeine and without antitussive action. Believed to have little addiction potential, it was widely sold in over-the-counter combinations with paracetamol. Overdose caused delirium and seizures, and its demethylated metabolite, which accumulates on repeated dosing, is cardiotoxic; deaths were reported. It was withdrawn in the UK, Europe and the USA and banned in India in 2013.

cards.front: Which drugs are used to manage opioid withdrawal and opioid use disorder?
cards.back: Agonist substitution: oral methadone (full agonist; start 20 to 30 mg for detoxification, or titrate to 60 to 80 mg daily for maintenance) or transmucosal buprenorphine (partial agonist, 4 to 16 mg daily, safer because of its ceiling on respiratory depression). Buprenorphine is combined with naloxone to deter injection, and patients must be off other opioids before starting it to avoid precipitated withdrawal. Symptom control: clonidine or lofexidine (central alpha-2 agonists) relieve autonomic withdrawal features but not aches or craving; postural hypotension is common. Relapse prevention: naltrexone, oral or monthly depot, after about 7 opioid-free days. Overdose: naloxone injection or nasal spray. Long-term maintenance gives better outcomes than detoxification alone.

cards.front: Anti-amyloid antibody therapy in Alzheimer disease: what is it, for whom, and how is safety monitored?
cards.back: Monoclonal antibodies against amyloid-beta clear amyloid plaques; aducanumab was the first approved (US accelerated approval, based on plaque reduction as a surrogate, and controversial because clinical benefit was not clearly shown). Use is limited to mild cognitive impairment or mild dementia due to AD, with amyloid confirmed by PET or CSF testing, since earlier stages respond better. It is given by monthly IV infusion. MRI is needed before starting and every 6 months because amyloid-related imaging abnormalities (ARIA) occurred in almost half of phase III patients. Earlier antibodies (bapineuzumab, solanezumab) failed in trials.

cards.front: Classify: disulfiram and disulfiram-like reactions
cards.text: Disulfiram irreversibly inhibits {{aldehyde dehydrogenase}}, so {{acetaldehyde}} accumulates after alcohol; a milder disulfiram-like reaction can occur with {{metronidazole}}, {{cefoperazone}} and {{sulfonylureas}}.

cards.front: Short note: Drugs acting via NMDA receptors

points: Excitatory glutamate receptor that gates calcium-selective cation channels in neurones
Ketamine and nitrous oxide inhibit it; volatile anaesthetics have little action here
Dissociative anaesthesia: profound analgesia, immobility and amnesia with light sleep
Acts on cortex and subcortical areas, not the reticular activating system
Respiration and airway reflexes preserved; BP, heart rate and cardiac output rise
Emergence reactions, hallucinations in up to half of patients during recovery
Avoid in hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure and raised intracranial pressure
NMDA antagonist that also promotes presynaptic dopamine release
Used in parkinsonism; tolerance develops over weeks to months
Non-competitive, use-dependent NMDA blocker that limits glutamate excitotoxicity
Slows functional decline in moderate-to-severe Alzheimer's disease
Better tolerated than anticholinesterases

cards.front: Short note: Recent advances in drug therapy of neurodegenerative disorders

points: Rasagiline: newer selective MAO-B inhibitor, about 5 times more potent and longer acting than selegiline
Rasagiline is not metabolised to amphetamine, so it avoids excitation and insomnia; now preferred over selegiline
Ropinirole and pramipexole: non-ergot dopamine agonists with less dyskinesia and motor fluctuation than levodopa
Entacapone (COMT inhibitor) prolongs levodopa action in advanced disease
Rivastigmine is also available as a 24-hour transdermal patch
Rivastigmine suits mild-to-moderate disease only
Memantine (NMDA blocker) for moderate-to-severe disease
These newer agents mainly give symptomatic benefit
Disease progression is not clearly altered
